audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht’s Computer Science bachelor combines programming, algorithms, mathematics and computer systems with team projects and an individual thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The Maastricht example follows the published 2025–2026 regulations. Some course listings differ in the separate catalogue, and later years may change. UCR offers related study in software, algorithms and data, or in AI and robotics. Maastricht includes additional specialist computing and project work.

curriculum.routeLabel: Intelligent Interaction, High Performance Computing and the Year 3 elective semester with Project 3-1

cellNotes.text: Both courses teach data types, control flow and procedures. UCR uses Python and Maastricht uses Java.
UCR builds programming and algorithmic skills across several courses. Maastricht combines an introductory survey with a microcontroller laboratory.
Introduction to Programming includes some object-oriented work. Maastricht offers a separate course covering classes, interfaces and polymorphism.
Both cover requirements, design, testing and maintenance. Maastricht also develops software architecture.
UCR uses C++ and Haskell for software development. Maastricht studies principles of programming languages in a separate course.
UCR covers object-oriented programming in its introductory Python course. Maastricht allocates a separate core course to object-oriented modelling.
Both teach algorithm design, data structures and performance analysis. The UCR course includes experimental performance analysis.
Both develop algorithmic design. UCR adds algebraic algorithms and optimisation. Maastricht covers greedy algorithms and dynamic programming.
Both develop discrete mathematical and logical tools for computing. Maastricht emphasises proof techniques.
UCR integrates logic into discrete mathematics. Maastricht teaches formal logic in a separate course.
Maastricht requires a separate course on computation and its theoretical limits.
Both develop differential and integral calculus. UCR also uses differential equations to build and analyse dynamic models.
Both teach systems of linear equations, matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations.
Both cover probability, distributions and statistical inference. UCR uses computer algebra for simulation.
Both cover numerical methods for roots and differential equations. UCR examines accuracy and stability.
UCR covers networks and operating systems together, including Internet protocols. Maastricht assigns separate courses to networks and operating systems.
Operating systems are covered alongside networks in one UCR course. Maastricht gives operating systems a separate place in Year 3.
Both teach relational databases and SQL. UCR also covers normalisation and query processing.
UCR introduces concurrency in operating systems. Maastricht devotes a separate course to parallel programming.
UCR Robotics develops motion and manipulation. Maastricht’s embedded programming course focuses on programming devices.
Maastricht requires a dedicated computer security course.
Maastricht combines high-performance computing with a dedicated semester project.
Both study intelligent agents and methods for search and problem solving.
Both cover image processing. Maastricht combines the course with a semester project in human-computer interaction.
UCR studies human perception and the ethics of intelligent systems. Maastricht teaches the design and evaluation of intelligent interfaces.
Both examine ethical questions raised by computing. The UCR course focuses on AI.
UCR covers parts of this area through AI Ethics and Strategy & Digital Transformation. Maastricht requires a dedicated IT management and privacy course.
Maastricht gives credit for a semester-long team project. UCR embeds project work in individual courses.
Maastricht requires a second team project that draws on concurrent computing courses.
Maastricht offers a semester-long team project for an external client.
Six elective courses provide space to broaden or deepen study. The example leaves individual choices open.
Maastricht requires an 18 EC thesis. UCR’s 15 EC independent research option sits outside the scheduled course comparison.

notes.text: Maastricht requires specialist work in computer security, embedded programming, parallel computing, programming-language principles and theory of computation. The selected High Performance Computing module adds a semester project. UCR offers related foundations in software development, networks, operating systems, mathematics and AI.

Maastricht builds from a common computing core to specialist modules, team projects and an individual thesis. UCR’s two options use elective courses to develop different emphases in computing or AI. Optional UCR independent research is separate from the scheduled courses.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENENTR212.name: Strategy & Digital Transformation
BENENTR212.text: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.

BENGATE101.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
BENGATE101.text: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.

DISARIN111.name: AI Ethics
DISARIN111.text: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

DISARIN211.name: Decision-making in AI
DISARIN211.text: Decision-making in AI examines how intelligent agents make decisions under uncertainty. Students study probability, Bayesian networks, temporal models, expected utility, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems. Multi-agent decisions and probabilistic programming extend the analysis, supported by equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.

DISARIN212.name: Logic & Discrete Mathematics
DISARIN212.text: Introduces formal logic, abstract reasoning and proof. Students work with propositions, quantified statements, sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, direct and indirect proofs, induction and recursion. A final component models processes and games without chance and investigates winning strategies.

DISARIN311.text: Optimization Methods in AI studies search and optimisation for rational agents. Topics include uninformed and heuristic search, local and global optimisation, adversarial search, constraint satisfaction, linear programming and discrete optimisation. Laboratory exercises and projects develop algorithm implementation, evaluation and experimental investigation of small intelligent systems.
